title: Crafting STAR Stories
summary: Turning real work experience into sharp, reusable STAR stories — picking the right memories, quantifying them, and pre-loading the follow-ups.

slides.markdown:
Knowing the STAR format doesn't automatically give you good stories to put in it. Most engineers have plenty of real work experience and still freeze when asked "tell me about a time you..." — not because nothing happened, but because they haven't done the work of turning raw memories into tight, reusable answers in advance.

This topic is that work: picking stories with real stakes, quantifying the result, mapping one story to several question types, and pre-loading the follow-ups an interviewer will ask. Do this once, well, before you interview, and you stop improvising under pressure — you're retrieving from a prepared bank instead.

slides.subTitle: A clear before versus after
slides.markdown:
Not every task makes a good STAR story, even if you did it well. The strongest candidates share one property: **a clear before-state and after-state that changed because of a decision you made** — not just a task that was completed.

Ask of any candidate memory: if I hadn't made this specific call, would the outcome plausibly have been worse or different? "I wrote the tests for the feature I was assigned" has no real stakes — someone would have written tests regardless. "I noticed our checkout error rate spiking during a deploy and rolled it back before the on-call page fired" has stakes: a different, plausible action (waiting for the page) leads to a worse outcome.

Good sources for high-stakes stories: incidents you responded to, a project you had to re-scope under a deadline, a technical disagreement you won or lost, a piece of legacy code you owned that was quietly failing. Routine, well-scoped ticket work rarely clears this bar on its own.

A single strong story usually answers several different prompts, depending on which part of it you emphasize. Take a production incident where you found and fixed a data corruption bug:

- Emphasize the debugging process → answers "tell me about a difficult technical problem."
- Emphasize convincing the team to delay a release to fix it properly → answers "tell me about a time you influenced a decision without authority."
- Emphasize the initial miscommunication with the reporting team → answers "tell me about a conflict with a coworker."
- Emphasize the root-cause writeup you pushed for afterward → answers "tell me about a time you improved a process."

This is why 6–10 well-chosen stories comfortably cover the 15–20 prompts a typical loop draws from — you're not memorizing 20 stories, you're memorizing 8 and knowing which lens to apply to each one live.

slides.subTitle: Numbers, scale, business impact
slides.markdown:
"It went well" is the single weakest sentence in a behavioral answer. Every Result should carry at least one number, and the number should map to something the business or the team actually cared about — not just an engineering vanity metric.

Weak → strong, same underlying fact:

- "Performance improved a lot" → "P99 latency on the search endpoint dropped from 800ms to 140ms, which took us under the 200ms SLO we'd been missing for two months."
- "We saved money" → "Right-sizing the batch cluster cut our nightly compute spend from roughly $4,200/month to $1,100/month."
- "The team was more productive" → "Deploy time went from 45 minutes to 6, so we went from 2 deploys a day to on-demand deploys."

If you genuinely don't have an exact number, an honest estimate beats a vague adjective: "roughly a third fewer support tickets" is still concrete. Never fabricate precision you don't have — a specific-sounding fake number is worse than an honest estimate, because a follow-up question will expose it.

slides.sectionTitle: The Action section is the interview
slides.markdown:
Everything before Action is scene-setting; everything the interviewer actually scores lives in Action. Specifically, they're listening for **decisions you made and the reasoning behind them** — not a chronological list of tasks.

Compare two ways of narrating the same work:

- Task list: "I looked at the logs, found the issue, wrote a fix, tested it, and deployed it."
- Decisions: "I suspected a race condition rather than a logic bug because the failure only showed up under load, so I reproduced it with a stress test instead of reading code first. Once confirmed, I chose a lock-free approach over a mutex because this path is on the hot request loop, even though it took longer to implement."

The second version shows *why*, at each branch point, which is the actual signal. Before an interview, go back through your story bank and underline every sentence that's a decision-with-reasoning versus a plain action — if a story is mostly the latter, it needs more digging before you use it.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: memory to STAR story
slides.markdown:
Raw memory: *"There was this thing where a teammate and I disagreed about whether to use a queue or just call the service directly, and we ended up going with the queue and it was fine."*

Tightened into a reusable STAR story:

- **Situation:** "We were adding a notification feature that had to call a third-party email API with a history of brief outages."
- **Task:** "I was designing the integration and a teammate wanted a direct synchronous call for simplicity."
- **Action:** "I proposed a queue instead, because a direct call would fail the whole request whenever the email API blipped. I prototyped both in about half a day, showed the teammate a load test where the direct-call version dropped 12% of requests during a simulated 30-second outage, and we agreed on the queue together."
- **Result:** "We shipped the queued version; three months later the email API had a 40-minute outage and zero user-facing failures — the messages just delayed and caught up."

Notice the vague version had no numbers and no visible decision process; the tightened version has both, and it took adding maybe four concrete details, not rewriting the story.

slides.subTitle: Pre-loading the details they'll ask for
slides.markdown:
For every story in your bank, write down the two or three follow-ups an interviewer is almost certain to ask, and pre-load the answer so you're not reconstructing it live:

- **"What did the other person say?"** — have an actual approximate quote or position ready, not "they understood eventually."
- **"Why that option and not the alternative?"** — have the rejected alternative named, plus the one or two-sentence reason.
- **"What would you do differently?"** — have one honest, specific answer prepared; "nothing, it went great" reads as a lack of self-awareness.
- **"How did you know it worked?"** — have the metric or verification step ready, not just the number itself.

This pre-loading is exactly what separates a fluent-sounding senior candidate from one who's clearly hearing the follow-up for the first time — the difference is almost never knowledge, it's preparation.

slides.sectionTitle: The story where your role disappears
slides.markdown:
A common failure at the story-bank stage: a story is genuinely impressive at the *team* level, but when you rehearse it, you can't isolate your specific contribution without it sounding like "I was there for the team's success."

Signs a story has this problem before you ever say it out loud: every sentence in your draft Action section starts with "we," you can't name a decision that was specifically yours, or removing yourself from the story wouldn't change how it reads.

The fix isn't to force an "I" into someone else's work — it's to either dig for the piece that genuinely was yours (there almost always is one, even on a big team project) or retire the story from your bank if it truly has no isolable individual contribution. A story bank with fewer, cleaner stories beats one padded with team-credit stories that collapse under "but what did *you* do?"

A story matrix maps your bank against common question categories, so retrieval during the interview is instant instead of a cold search:

| Story | Conflict | Failure | Leadership | Ambiguity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Email-queue design disagreement | Primary | — | Secondary | — |
| Data-corruption incident | Secondary | Primary | Secondary | — |
| Migrating a legacy billing job with no docs | — | — | — | Primary |
| Convincing another team to adopt a shared library | — | — | Primary | Secondary |

"Primary" means that's the story's best fit for that category; "Secondary" means it works but isn't the strongest option. Building this table once, before interviewing, turns "tell me about a conflict" from a search into a lookup — you already know your top pick and your backup.

slides.sectionTitle: A story with range versus a single-use story
slides.markdown:
Some stories only ever answer one question well; others have genuine range. The difference is usually how many distinct decision points the story contains.

- **Single-use:** "I fixed a flaky test that was blocking CI." One decision point (diagnose and fix), so it only really answers "tell me about a technical problem you solved."
- **High-range:** "I led the migration off a deprecated payments SDK." Multiple decision points — how to sequence the migration with zero downtime, how to get a skeptical stakeholder to prioritize it, how to handle a partial rollback when one integration broke — so it can answer ambiguity, influence, and failure/recovery questions depending on emphasis.

When choosing which 6–10 stories to invest prep time in, prefer high-range stories over single-use ones — you get more coverage per story memorized, and less risk of running out of material deep into a loop.

A story bank goes stale the same way any inventory does. Two habits keep it useful:

- **Add a story within a week of it happening**, while the numbers and the follow-up details are still fresh — reconstructing "was it a 15% or 20% drop" a year later is much harder than jotting it down immediately after a retro or incident review.
- **Prune stories that no longer match your level.** A story that was your strongest "leadership" answer as a mid-level engineer may read as too small in scope once you're interviewing for staff roles — keep it if it still shows real judgment, retire it if it now reads as junior-scoped.

Treat the bank as a living document you revisit every few months, not a one-time exercise before a specific interview — the cost of updating it in real time is minutes; the cost of reconstructing three years of history the night before an onsite is not.
